assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock work and the task-based account of labour demand changed how economists and policymakers understand trade, technology, local labour markets and wage inequality. The designs are credible and the findings have affected policy debate far beyond economics.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock papers are most clearly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Autor's task-approach work overlaps with Katz, Goldin and Acemoglu, so credit is somewhat entangled with already-honoured work. A trio of Autor, Hanson and Dorn is coherent and leaves Katz out.
assessment.maturity: The core papers are from 2013 to 2016 and have more than a decade of replication, extension and debate. The finding is mature enough, though some persistence and magnitude results are still being refined.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior prizes for labour economics and technology (Card, Goldin, Acemoglu).
Debate over how large and how persistent the local effects are, and over shift-share identification.
Whether Katz's role should replace Dorn or Hanson.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their work shows with granular data that household leverage and credit supply drive housing booms, consumption collapses and recessions. It reshaped macro-finance and post-crisis policy thinking. The empirical approach is credible and the effect on macroeconomics has been large.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the clear, tightly linked core pair. Campbell contributes household finance but not this specific discovery, so I would not add him.
assessment.maturity: The key papers date from 2009 to 2014 and the book House of Debt is from 2014. The ideas have been tested widely and have entered policy and textbooks. The 2022 prize for banking and crises is adjacent but distinct.
uncertainties: Possible perceived overlap with the 2022 Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig prize.
Some county-level and zip-code evidence has been contested on mechanisms.
Relative standing against other crisis-related macro work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection brought a new foundation to trade theory and shifted empirical work to micro data. It established the productivity-based channel for gains from trade and strongly influenced trade, growth and IO research.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman has strong related work with Melitz and Yeaple, and Redding's role is more recent and quantitative. Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers the intellectual lineage but not this development.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of theoretical and empirical development have followed. The framework is standard in graduate teaching and policy modelling.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among Melitz, Helpman, Bernard, Eaton, Kortum and others outside the list.
Overlap with the Krugman prize.
Whether the quantitative gains-from-trade results are sensitive to model structure.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Manning's work on monopsony and dynamic labour-market frictions changed the view of wage-setting, minimum wages and employer power. It is conceptually important and policy relevant, and it connects to a broad modern literature.
assessment.attribution: Manning is the clear intellectual centre through Monopsony in Motion. Ashenfelter and Naidu contribute adjacent empirical work but are not core to the monopsony framework itself. Card and Krueger already have a prize for related minimum-wage evidence.
assessment.maturity: The framework has strengthened since the early 2000s, and evidence of labour-market concentration and wage markdowns has expanded. It is not yet fully settled, since estimates of markdowns vary.
uncertainties: Estimates of employer power vary across settings and methods.
Overlap with the 2021 Card prize and with other labour-search theory.
A single-laureate prize is possible but unusual.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income series built from tax records transformed the empirical study of inequality and public debate. The data and measurement contribution is high, though the theoretical claims (r>g) are contested.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the founding pair for the top-income series. Zucman's wealth and offshore-wealth contributions are important but later and more contested. The contributions are partly data infrastructure and rely on many collaborators.
assessment.maturity: The series date from the early 2000s and have been extended and replicated across countries. Methodological debates, such as the treatment of taxes and transfers, continue.
uncertainties: Controversy over the wealth-inequality methods and the theory in Capital in the Twenty-First Century.
Whether data construction fits the prize better than a conceptual discovery.
Political salience may affect deliberation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal effects, including causal forests and double or debiased ML, gave economists valid inference with high-dimensional data and heterogeneous effects. The influence on applied work is growing quickly.
assessment.attribution: Athey (with Wager and Imbens) and Chernozhukov (with Chetverikov, Demirer, Duflo, Hansen, Newey and Robins) have distinct but related contributions. Credit is spread across a large community, and Imbens's 2021 prize already honours part of the area.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from 2016 to 2018. Adoption is rapid but the field is young and still evolving, so the prize may be premature.
uncertainties: Attribution across many co-authors, including Newey, Hansen, Duflo and Imbens.
Maturity: lasting empirical impact is still being established.
Overlap with the 2021 prize for causal inference.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: HANK models put household heterogeneity into monetary and fiscal transmission and changed how macro models are built and used for policy. The approach is influential in central banks and research.
assessment.attribution: Kaplan, Moll and Violante are the natural trio through the 2018 AER paper and related work. The methodological lineage also draws on Aiyagari, Huggett, Krusell and Smith and on Auclert and others.
assessment.maturity: The core work is from 2014 to 2018 and many extensions are recent. It is promising but the long-run test is incomplete.
uncertainties: The field is still young.
Credit to Auclert, Bayer, Kaplan-Violante and earlier heterogeneous-agent pioneers.
Empirical validation of transmission channels is ongoing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Models of present bias and reference dependence are central to behavioural economics and shape work on savings, health and consumer protection. They are conceptually rich and have strong evidence behind them.
assessment.attribution: Laibson (quasi-hyperbolic discounting), Rabin (psychology-informed theory) and Koszegi (with Rabin, reference-dependent preferences) have clear and distinct contributions. O'Donoghue and Loewenstein add to the broader area. Kahneman and Thaler already received prizes for related behavioural foundations.
assessment.maturity: The ideas are decades old and widely applied. Some field evidence on loss aversion and reference points is mixed.
uncertainties: Overlap with the Kahneman (2002) and Thaler (2017) prizes.
Heterogeneous replication of loss aversion and reference-point effects in field settings.
How to allocate credit among five listed names.
